This tutorial starts with elevations at known coordinates, builds a digital elevation model (DEM), and calculates topographical variables used in forest ecology. The outputs describe local terrain, exposure, relative position and potential drainage. They can later be assigned to trees, quadrats or other areas.

The general input is a table with `x`, `y` and `z`: two horizontal coordinates and elevation. These values may come from a survey, a data provider or other instruments. Section 1 obtains them from the example survey of height differences. It is optional: users who already have elevations can start at section 2. Users with a DEM can skip interpolation as well.

The main workflow uses two packages:

-   **terra:** raster objects, local terrain calculations, maps and GeoTIFF files. The main object is a `SpatRaster`, with one layer per variable.
-   **whitebox:** curvature and hydrological calculations. It calls the separate WhiteboxTools program, which needs a one-time installation. Zhang et al. (2025) also used terra and whitebox for tropical forest terrain calculations.

An optional third package, **interp**, provides the linear and spline alternatives shown in section 2. It is not needed for the default interpolation.

Raster layers and GeoTIFF files can also hold other environmental variables. This is useful when topography is later combined with soil, canopy or disturbance data. A separate tutorial will cover combining these sources and extracting values for points or polygons.

**Setup and parameters**

Keep the main choices together. The example uses local coordinates in metres, with `y` increasing northward. These are not longitude and latitude. For a real site, retain its actual coordinate system and check the orientation of its grid.

```{r}
#| label: setup-terrain
#| results: hide

# install.packages(c("terra", "whitebox"))
# install.packages("interp")  # Only for the optional linear or spline interpolation.
# whitebox::install_whitebox()  # Once, to install the WhiteboxTools program.

library(terra)

path.to.fgeo2 = if(file.exists("../../fgeo2.Rproj")) "../.." else "."
# path.to.fgeo2 = "/full/path/to/fgeo2"

reference.xy = c(0, 0)
reference.z = 371
plot.extent = c(0, 240, 0, 240)  # xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, in metres.
cell.size = 5
interpolation = "idw"          # "idw", "linear" or "akima".
search.radius = 60             # IDW search radius, in metres.
idw.power = 2                  # Distance weighting: larger values favour nearer points.
idw.smooth = 0                 # IDW distance-smoothing parameter, in metres.
smoothing.cells = 3            # Odd window width; 1 means no smoothing.
position.radius = 20           # TPI neighbourhood radius, in metres.
breach.distance.cells = 20     # Maximum search distance for drainage preparation.
channel.area.m2 = 1000         # Illustrative channel threshold; check in the field.

# Temporary by default. Change this to keep the files after the R session.
output.dir = file.path(tempdir(), "fgeo2-topography")
# output.dir = "/full/path/to/save/topography"
dir.create(output.dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
output.dir <- normalizePath(output.dir, winslash = "/")

# Reuse these settings in the maps below.
map.colors = hcl.colors(50, "Viridis")
signed.colors = hcl.colors(51, "Blue-Red 3", rev = TRUE)
aspect.colors = hcl.colors(36, "Dynamic")
map.margins = c(3, 3, 2, 4)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.width = 6, fig.height = 5)
whitebox::wbt_verbose(FALSE)
```

# From height differences to point elevations

Skip this section if a provider has already supplied an `{x, y, z}` table. The rest of the tutorial does not depend on how those elevations were obtained.

For this example, positive `dz` means that the destination is higher than the origin. The reference point sets the elevation datum. See [the solver tutorial](topography-solver.qmd) for the survey and its checks. The solver also needs Matrix and igraph.

```{r}
#| label: survey-to-elevations

records <- read.csv(file.path(path.to.fgeo2, "data_examples/topography-survey.csv"))
survey <- data.frame(
	x_i = records$from_x_m,
	y_i = records$from_y_m,
	x_j = records$to_x_m,
	y_j = records$to_y_m,
	dz = records$height_difference_m
)

source(file.path(path.to.fgeo2, "06_topography_habitat/R/new/topography-solver.R"))
elevations <- estimate_point_elevations(survey, reference.xy, reference.z)
head(elevations)

# General entry point when elevations come from elsewhere:
# elevations <- read.csv("/full/path/to/point-elevations.csv")
# names(elevations) must include x, y and z, in compatible metre units.
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-point-elevations
#| fig-cap: "Point elevations used to build the DEM. No regular input grid is required."

elevation.points <- vect(elevations, geom = c("x", "y"), crs = "local")
plot(elevation.points, "z", pch = 16, cex = 0.6, col = map.colors,
     main = "Point elevations (m)", axes = TRUE, mar = map.margins)
```

# Build the DEM

The DEM represents ground elevation. A surface that follows the canopy is a different input and should not be used as ground topography.

Use one finite elevation per distinct coordinate pair. Resolve missing or conflicting records before interpolation.

The main choices are:

-   **Resolution:** `cell.size` sets the output spacing. A 5 m raster does not create 5 m measured detail from a survey taken mostly at 20 m intervals.
-   **Interpolation:** the default inverse-distance weighting (IDW) gives nearby points more weight. Its search radius, distance power and smoothing parameter are declared above. `linear` connects the elevations with planar triangles; `akima` gives a smoother surface, which may overshoot the observed range. The last two options need interp.
-   **Smoothing:** `smoothing.cells` sets a moving mean applied before the derivatives. At 5 m resolution, a width of 3 covers 15 m. Use 1 to keep the interpolated DEM unchanged. Compare choices before interpreting small ridges or depressions.

Raster coordinates refer to cell centres. A 5 m raster over 0--240 m has centres at 2.5, 7.5, ..., 237.5 m. Interpolating at those centres keeps the raster boundary at the plot boundary.

```{r}
#| label: construct-dem

dem <- rast(xmin = plot.extent[1], xmax = plot.extent[2],
            ymin = plot.extent[3], ymax = plot.extent[4],
            resolution = cell.size, crs = "local")
cell.xy <- xyFromCell(dem, seq_len(ncell(dem)))

if(!interpolation %in% c("idw", "linear", "akima")) stop("Unknown interpolation method.")
if(interpolation == "idw")
	dem <- interpIDW(dem, as.matrix(elevations[c("x", "y", "z")]),
	                  radius = search.radius, power = idw.power, smooth = idw.smooth,
	                  minPoints = 3, maxPoints = 12)
if(interpolation %in% c("linear", "akima"))
	values(dem) <- interp::interp(
		x = elevations$x, y = elevations$y, z = elevations$z,
		xo = cell.xy[, 1], yo = cell.xy[, 2],
		method = interpolation, output = "points"
	)$z

# A complete regular input grid can instead use bilinear resampling:
# grid.dem <- rast(elevations[c("x", "y", "z")], type = "xyz", crs = "local")
# dem <- resample(grid.dem, dem, method = "bilinear")

# Retain only cell centres inside the observed points' convex hull.
dem <- mask(dem, convHull(elevation.points), touches = FALSE)

if(smoothing.cells > 1)
	dem <- focal(dem, w = smoothing.cells, fun = "mean", na.rm = TRUE, na.policy = "omit")
names(dem) <- "elevation_m"
```

The mask leaves cells outside the observed points' convex hull as `NA`. Smoothing preserves those missing cells and uses available neighbours at the boundary. Check the DEM for gaps and interpolation artefacts before continuing. If linear interpolation leaves interior gaps, use IDW or the complete-grid alternative. For larger sites, keep the terrain surrounding the plot until after the calculations.

```{r}
#| label: fig-dem
#| fig-cap: "Interpolated DEM after the selected smoothing. Points show the input locations."

plot(dem, col = map.colors, main = "Elevation (m)",
     axes = TRUE, mar = map.margins)
points(elevation.points, pch = 16, cex = 0.2)

# Alternative entry point when a ground DEM is already available:
# dem <- rast("/full/path/to/elevation.tif")
# Keep its actual CRS and native resolution. Derivatives need compatible units.
```

The complete workflow below assumes square raster cells and horizontal and vertical units in metres. When using an existing DEM, use an appropriate metre-based projected CRS. Do not label longitude and latitude coordinates as metres.

# Derive topographical variables

These are complementary descriptions of the same terrain. They are often correlated; calculating them all does not mean that all should enter the same statistical model.

-   **Elevation:** height relative to the chosen datum.
-   **Slope:** terrain inclination.
-   **Aspect, northness and eastness:** orientation of the slope, with two continuous components for analysis.
-   **Topographic position (TPI):** height relative to a stated neighbourhood; a local description of ridges and depressions.
-   **Terrain ruggedness (TRI):** local elevation differences.
-   **Plan and profile curvature:** changes in surface direction and slope.
-   **Contributing area:** terrain supplying runoff to each location.
-   **Topographic wetness index (TWI):** potential for water accumulation from contributing area and slope.
-   **Downslope distance to drainage:** distance along the drainage route.
-   **Height above drainage:** vertical separation from the drainage reached downhill.

Recent forest studies use aspect components and ruggedness (McNichol et al. 2024; Freund et al. 2021), and wetness indices (Zhang et al. 2025). Curvature and drainage position also have applications to forest structure and floristic composition (Detto et al. 2013; Schietti et al. 2014).

Spatial scale is part of each variable. DEM resolution, smoothing and neighbourhood size can change the results (Detto et al. 2013; Muscarella et al. 2020). Blank boundary cells are retained where the full local neighbourhood is unavailable.

## Elevation

Elevation is already in the DEM. It can describe broad gradients within a plot, although it does not directly measure soil moisture or soil fertility. An arbitrary elevation datum is sufficient for the relative terrain calculations below.

```{r}
#| label: fig-elevation-layer

elevation <- dem
plot(elevation, col = map.colors, main = "Elevation (m)",
     axes = TRUE, mar = map.margins)
```

## Slope

Slope is the inclination from horizontal, in degrees. It describes steepness and is often used when analysing forest structure or disturbance. Here, terra uses the elevations in the eight neighbouring cells.

```{r}
#| label: fig-slope

slope <- terrain(dem, v = "slope", unit = "degrees", neighbors = 8)
names(slope) <- "slope_deg"
plot(slope, col = map.colors, main = "Slope (degrees)",
     axes = TRUE, mar = map.margins)
```

## Aspect, northness and eastness

Aspect is the downhill direction, clockwise from north. It can represent differences in exposure, as in the Niobrara ForestGEO study of microclimate (McNichol et al. 2024). On our local grid, this interpretation assumes that positive `y` points north.

Northness and eastness avoid the discontinuity between 359 and 0 degrees: they are the cosine and sine of aspect. Flat cells have no meaningful aspect and are left blank.

```{r}
#| label: fig-aspect-components
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4

aspect <- terrain(dem, v = "aspect", unit = "degrees", neighbors = 8)
aspect[slope == 0] <- NA
northness <- cos(aspect * pi / 180)
eastness <- sin(aspect * pi / 180)
names(aspect) <- "aspect_deg"
names(northness) <- "northness"
names(eastness) <- "eastness"

settings <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
plot(aspect, col = aspect.colors, range = c(0, 360), main = "Aspect (degrees)", mar = map.margins)
plot(northness, col = signed.colors, range = c(-1, 1), main = "Northness", mar = map.margins)
plot(eastness, col = signed.colors, range = c(-1, 1), main = "Eastness", mar = map.margins)
par(settings)
```

## Topographic position (TPI)

TPI is focal elevation minus the mean elevation of its neighbours. Positive values indicate locally higher ground; negative values indicate depressions. The neighbourhood below is a square extending `position.radius` metres from the focal cell centre, rounded up to a whole number of cells.

This is analogous to an elevation-difference convexity measure. It does not reproduce the CTFS quadrat calculation or its perimeter convention. The focal unit here is a raster cell, and the scale is explicit.

```{r}
#| label: fig-tpi

radius.cells <- ceiling(position.radius / res(dem)[1])
weights <- matrix(1, 2 * radius.cells + 1, 2 * radius.cells + 1)
weights[radius.cells + 1, radius.cells + 1] <- NA  # Exclude the focal cell.
tpi <- dem - focal(dem, w = weights, fun = "mean", na.rm = FALSE)
names(tpi) <- "tpi_m"
tpi.limit <- global(abs(tpi), "max", na.rm = TRUE)[1, 1]
plot(tpi, col = signed.colors, range = c(-tpi.limit, tpi.limit),
     main = "Topographic position (m)", axes = TRUE, mar = map.margins)
```

## Terrain ruggedness (TRI)

This TRI is the mean absolute elevation difference between a cell and its eight neighbours, in metres. Freund et al. (2021) used this definition in a study of forest recovery after landslides. It measures local relief and can be strongly related to slope.

```{r}
#| label: fig-tri

tri <- terrain(dem, v = "TRI")
names(tri) <- "tri_m"
plot(tri, col = map.colors, main = "Terrain ruggedness (m)",
     axes = TRUE, mar = map.margins)
```

## Curvature

Plan curvature describes convergence or divergence across the slope. Profile curvature describes how steepness changes downhill. These are second derivatives of elevation and are particularly sensitive to interpolation and smoothing. Detto et al. (2013) used several curvature measures to describe forest canopy structure in Panama.

The WhiteboxTools 2.4.0 implementation used here reports curvature in inverse metres. Positive plan curvature indicates divergence; positive profile curvature indicates acceleration of downhill flow. The two signs describe different things. These are not the CTFS convexity measure. The calculation uses a 5 by 5 cell fit; the incomplete boundary is masked below.

```{r}
#| label: fig-curvature
#| results: hide
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.5

dem.file <- file.path(output.dir, "elevation.tif")
plan.file <- file.path(output.dir, "plan-curvature.tif")
profile.file <- file.path(output.dir, "profile-curvature.tif")
writeRaster(dem, dem.file, overwrite = TRUE)
whitebox::wbt_plan_curvature(dem.file, plan.file, log = FALSE, zfactor = 1)
whitebox::wbt_profile_curvature(dem.file, profile.file, log = FALSE, zfactor = 1)
plan.curvature <- rast(plan.file)
profile.curvature <- rast(profile.file)
support <- focal(!is.na(dem), w = 5, fun = "sum", fillvalue = 0)
plan.curvature[support < 25] <- NA
profile.curvature[support < 25] <- NA
names(plan.curvature) <- "plan_curvature_per_m"
names(profile.curvature) <- "profile_curvature_per_m"
plan.limit <- global(abs(plan.curvature), "max", na.rm = TRUE)[1, 1]
profile.limit <- global(abs(profile.curvature), "max", na.rm = TRUE)[1, 1]

settings <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(plan.curvature, col = signed.colors, range = c(-plan.limit, plan.limit),
     main = "Plan curvature (1/m)", mar = map.margins)
plot(profile.curvature, col = signed.colors, range = c(-profile.limit, profile.limit),
     main = "Profile curvature (1/m)", mar = map.margins)
par(settings)
```

## Contributing area

Contributing area describes how much upslope terrain supplies flow to a cell. It is an input to TWI. The D-infinity method below can divide flow between neighbouring directions. The specific contributing area (SCA) is area per unit contour width, in metres; multiplying by cell width gives the corresponding area in square metres.

Flow routing needs a draining surface. A separate copy of the DEM is prepared by breaching depressions, with filling where breaching fails. Inspect this choice where depressions are real features. The earlier local terrain layers still use the original DEM.

**The example covers only the plot.** It omits water arriving from outside. The following drainage maps demonstrate the workflow, but are not complete catchment estimates. For ecological analysis, use surrounding terrain and delineated drainage appropriate to the site; Muscarella et al. (2020) explicitly tested DEM extent and resolution.

```{r}
#| label: fig-contributing-area
#| results: hide

hydro.file <- file.path(output.dir, "elevation-for-flow.tif")
sca.file <- file.path(output.dir, "specific-contributing-area.tif")
whitebox::wbt_breach_depressions_least_cost(
	dem.file, hydro.file, dist = breach.distance.cells, fill = TRUE
)
whitebox::wbt_d_inf_flow_accumulation(
	input = hydro.file, output = sca.file,
	out_type = "Specific Contributing Area", log = FALSE
)
sca <- rast(sca.file)
contributing.area <- sca * res(dem)[1]
names(contributing.area) <- "contributing_area_m2"
plot(log10(contributing.area), col = map.colors,
     main = "Contributing area: log10(m2)", axes = TRUE, mar = map.margins)
```

## Topographic wetness index (TWI)

TWI combines specific contributing area and local slope: `log(SCA / tan(slope))`. Higher values indicate greater topographic potential for water accumulation. It is a proxy, not measured soil moisture. Zhang et al. (2025) used TWI to describe tropical forest canopy dynamics.

Whitebox expects **unlogged SCA and slope in degrees**. It converts the angle internally. Zero-slope cells become `NA`. Here, slope comes from the same DEM used for the local terrain variables; only the flow-routing surface was conditioned.

```{r}
#| label: fig-twi
#| results: hide

slope.file <- file.path(output.dir, "slope.tif")
twi.file <- file.path(output.dir, "twi.tif")
writeRaster(slope, slope.file, overwrite = TRUE)
whitebox::wbt_wetness_index(sca.file, slope.file, twi.file)
twi <- rast(twi.file)
names(twi) <- "twi"
plot(twi, col = map.colors, main = "Topographic wetness index",
     axes = TRUE, mar = map.margins)
```

## Downslope distance to drainage

This is distance along the downhill flow path to a channel, not straight-line distance to the closest channel. Detto et al. (2013) related flow distance to canopy height.

A channel network must first be defined. The example uses a D8 contributing-area threshold, in square metres. Change `channel.area.m2` to reflect site hydrology and check it against mapped channels. This synthetic network does not identify observed or perennial streams.

```{r}
#| label: fig-drainage-distance
#| results: hide

d8.area.file <- file.path(output.dir, "d8-contributing-area.tif")
streams.file <- file.path(output.dir, "drainage.tif")
distance.file <- file.path(output.dir, "distance-to-drainage.tif")
whitebox::wbt_d8_flow_accumulation(hydro.file, d8.area.file,
                                  out_type = "catchment area", log = FALSE)
whitebox::wbt_extract_streams(d8.area.file, streams.file,
                             threshold = channel.area.m2, zero_background = TRUE)
whitebox::wbt_downslope_distance_to_stream(
	hydro.file, streams.file, distance.file, dinf = FALSE
)
drainage.distance <- rast(distance.file)
names(drainage.distance) <- "drainage_distance_m"
plot(drainage.distance, col = map.colors, main = "Downslope distance to drainage (m)",
     axes = TRUE, mar = map.margins)
```

The D8 network routes flow to one neighbour; it is used consistently for the drainage distance and height below. TWI uses the distributed D-infinity accumulation. These are separate, visible choices. Cells whose route leaves the DEM without reaching a defined channel can remain blank.

## Height above drainage

This is elevation relative to the channel reached along the downhill flow path. It is often called HAND: height above the nearest drainage. Here, "nearest" refers to the drainage route, not the shortest map distance. Schietti et al. (2014) used HAND to describe floristic composition in an Amazonian forest.

HAND can distinguish terrain near valley bottoms from higher slopes. It is not a direct measurement of groundwater depth. The channel threshold and the extent of the DEM remain important.

```{r}
#| label: fig-height-above-drainage
#| results: hide

hand.file <- file.path(output.dir, "height-above-drainage.tif")
whitebox::wbt_elevation_above_stream(hydro.file, streams.file, hand.file)
hand <- rast(hand.file)
names(hand) <- "height_above_drainage_m"
plot(hand, col = map.colors, main = "Height above drainage (m)",
     axes = TRUE, mar = map.margins)
```

# Keep the layers and save GeoTIFF files

These layers share a grid because they were derived from the same DEM. Combine them into one `SpatRaster`, retaining descriptive names and units. GeoTIFF stores the grid, coordinates and values in a format that other GIS tools can read.

```{r}
#| label: save-topography

topography <- c(elevation, slope, aspect, northness, eastness, tpi, tri,
                 plan.curvature, profile.curvature, contributing.area,
                 twi, drainage.distance, hand)
units(topography) <- c("m", "degrees", "degrees", "1", "1", "m", "m",
                       "1/m", "1/m", "m2", "1", "m", "m")

writeRaster(topography, file.path(output.dir, "topography.tif"),
            datatype = "FLT4S", gdal = "COMPRESS=LZW", overwrite = TRUE)
write.csv(data.frame(variable = names(topography), unit = units(topography)),
          file.path(output.dir, "topography-layers.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

# Read the saved layers in another R session.
saved.topography <- rast(file.path(output.dir, "topography.tif"))
names(saved.topography)

# Record the software used, including the separate WhiteboxTools program.
R.version.string
sapply(c("terra", "whitebox"), function(package) as.character(packageVersion(package)))
# packageVersion("interp")  # If used for interpolation.
print(whitebox::wbt_version())
```

Use a real persistent `output.dir` to keep these files. The local-coordinate example retains a local Cartesian CRS; it is not a geographically positioned map. A real site's GeoTIFF should retain its actual CRS.

The same raster format can later hold soil, canopy and other environmental layers. Those data do not have to share this resolution or grid. Combining them, extracting values and assigning habitats are separate workflows.

Software documentation: [terra](https://rspatial.github.io/terra/reference/index.html), [interp](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/interp/refman/interp.html), and [whitebox](https://whiteboxr.gishub.org/reference/index.html). Curvature definitions were checked against the [WhiteboxTools 2.4.0 plan-curvature source](https://github.com/jblindsay/whitebox-tools/blob/v2.4.0/whitebox-tools-app/src/tools/terrain_analysis/plan_curvature.rs) and [profile-curvature source](https://github.com/jblindsay/whitebox-tools/blob/v2.4.0/whitebox-tools-app/src/tools/terrain_analysis/prof_curvature.rs).
